name: Belt pulling (CCW rotation bonesmash)

lead: Belt pulling is a looksmaxxing routine in which a person grips a belt in the mouth and applies body-weight force upward and forward. Proponents say this rotates the maxilla counterclockwise, which in their account shortens the midface, supports the under-eye area and brings the lower jaw forward.

It is discussed alongside towel pulling, thumb pulling and mewing as a non-surgical alternative to jaw surgery. Orthodontists use supervised facemask devices on growing children for related goals, but no published trial has tested the belt method.

paras: Forum descriptions involve a belt hung from a fixed point near mouth height, biting it, tucking the chin and loading body weight. Proponents pair it with proper tongue posture and say results take months. These accounts are not endorsed here.

Forum users report cracking sounds in the jaw, nausea, and teeth moving forward rather than any visible bone change. Commenters on looksmax.org warn that teeth shift far more easily than bone. Orthodontic headgear itself has reported side effects, including tooth soreness and, rarely, eye injuries, and is fitted by professionals.

angle.text: Proponents use it to try to reshape the upper jaw without surgery. Their stated aim is a shorter midface, more under-eye support and a more forward mandible.

lead: Belt pulling, also written about as counterclockwise (CCW) maxillary rotation, is a do-it-yourself routine from looksmaxxing forums. Participants grip a belt in the mouth and apply body-weight traction in an attempt to rotate the upper jaw so that its back moves up and its front moves forward, which they describe as counterclockwise when viewed from the side.[1] It is grouped with towel pulling, thumb pulling and zygomatic pulling as a kind of 'face pulling,' and with the wider set of 'bonesmashing' or bone-remodelling practices.[1][2]

The appeal is a change in facial proportions without surgery. Proponents say a downward-rotated maxilla produces a long midface, weak under-eye support and a recessed-looking jaw, and that rotating it up and forward would fill the midface, shorten its apparent length and bring the lower jaw forward.[1][2] They present belt pulling as a free alternative to bimaxillary surgery and as a stronger version of mewing, usually paired with tongue posture.[1][2]

No clinical study has tested belt pulling. The closest professional counterpart is the orthodontic facemask, which orthodontists fit to growing children to encourage forward growth of the upper jaw and whose results have been examined in systematic reviews.[3][4][4] Dermatologists, surgeons and orthodontic bodies have commented on related practices such as bonesmashing and mewing, saying there is no evidence they remodel facial bone.[5][6][7]

paras: Forum guides describe the routine in terms of a belt anchored high, such as on a pull-up bar, that the user bites while loading body weight. One guide's author says it must be paired with proper tongue posture to hold results and calls it more effective than other face-pulling techniques for counterclockwise rotation.[1] This article does not reproduce the step-by-step instructions.

A second thread lays out the theory behind it: that a maxilla rotated downward lengthens the midface, removes under-eye support and swings the jaw backward, so rotating the maxilla up and forward addresses all three. The poster calls the method an extreme version of mewing, asks whether it is safe, and wonders whether to start with thumb pulling and move to towel or belt pulling later.[2]

The practice sits within looksmaxxing, which Wikipedia says emerged in manosphere and incel communities in the 2010s around the PSL forums and spread to TikTok in the early 2020s.[7] Belt pulling itself appears in looksmax.org threads, where guides, 'tried it' reports and discussion of alternatives to bimaxillary surgery circulate.[1][8][2]

It shares a conceptual root with mewing, the tongue-posture practice developed by British orthodontist John Mew under the name orthotropics and publicised by his son Mike Mew. Interest in mewing began rising in January 2019, The Guardian covered it as a YouTube craze in March 2019, and the topic reached mainstream press and schools by 2024.[9] Mike Mew was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and, in 2024, struck from the UK dental register, according to Wikipedia.[9]

A related family of trends, bonesmashing, involves striking the face with blunt objects. Wikipedia describes it as an inside joke that is rarely done, while the American Academy of Dermatology and Vice, in a March 2026 article, document it as a social media trend and describe its risks.[5][6][7] Belt pulling is traction rather than impact, but forum threads and media discussions often place the two among the same bone-remodelling practices.

Proponents say belt pulling can fill the midface, lower the face's apparent length and help with malocclusion.[1] They describe the maxilla as capable of being moved over months or years by chewing, tongue posture and pulling, and some call it a free alternative to bimaxillary osteotomy.[2]

The reasoning appeals to the idea that bone adapts to load. The principle, usually attributed to German surgeon Julius Wolff in the nineteenth century and called Wolff's law, states that bone remodels in response to the loads it carries; Wikipedia notes that cyclic loading is the kind reported to drive bone formation.[10] The American Academy of Dermatology describes the application of this idea to blunt facial trauma as a misapplication of Wolff's law.[5]

Forum descriptions involve traction applied through the teeth with the head braced, usually combined with attention to tongue posture and sometimes with chewing exercises. Users in the threads say results take months or years.[1][2] Because the force passes through the teeth, commenters stress that it can move teeth instead of bone and that the method is unsupervised.[8][2]

Orthodontists use a facemask or reverse-pull headgear, with elastics attached to braces and anchored on pads at the forehead and chin, to encourage forward growth of the maxilla in Class III cases. It is used mainly in children and adolescents, typically between about 7 and 13 years of age, and is fitted and adjusted by an orthodontist.[3] Wikipedia describes the bar as worn for 14 to 16 hours a day and cites a 2016 randomised trial titled to say early facemask treatment reduces the need for orthognathic surgery.[11] Wikipedia notes that such devices effectively pull the teeth forward and lists side effects including tooth soreness, eye injuries with improper use, and reports of breathing and jaw joint problems.[3]

A 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis in Orthodontics & Craniofacial Research included three randomised trials with 155 growing patients, 92 treated and 63 controls. It reported short-term skeletal change, with the maxilla moving forward, the mandible moving backward, and a counterclockwise rotation of the maxillary plane alongside a clockwise rotation of the mandibular plane.[4] The orthodontic literature therefore uses the phrase counterclockwise rotation for a measured angle in supervised treatment of growing patients.

A 2023 systematic review of 14 studies on stability reported that the maxillary changes were stable in the short term and that the maxilla remained stable long term, while mandibular growth during the adolescent growth spurt continued unfavourably and was the main factor in long-term outcomes. It also reported proclined incisors and soft tissue changes that were minor.[4] Both reviews concern children treated by clinicians with purpose-built appliances, not adult traction routines.

Orthognathic or corrective jaw surgery cuts and repositions the jaws, usually in both the upper and lower jaw, and is used for dentofacial deformities that orthodontics cannot correct, with the aim of improving function and appearance.[12] Wikipedia estimates that such deformities affect nearly 5 percent of the UK and US population, gives initial healing as about 2 to 6 weeks, and lists infection, bleeding and nerve numbness among the risks.[12] Forum posters who promote pulling describe it as a way to avoid surgery of this kind.[2]

Palatal expanders widen the upper jaw and are most effective in children and adolescents; after puberty the midpalatal suture fuses, and expansion then requires surgical assistance or mini-implants that anchor force to bone instead of teeth.[13] This anchoring distinction mirrors the forum comment that force on the teeth moves teeth rather than the skeletal bone.[2][13]

One forum user who tried the method for a minute with strong force reported that only the back teeth moved forward and the lips looked wider briefly, with a cracking sound in the jaw and nausea.[8] Other commenters wrote that force anchored on the teeth moves teeth far more easily than skeletal bone and that the method is dangerous without professional guidance.[2] Some replies call the approach sketchy or likely to cause injury.[1]

For the related bonesmashing trend, the American Academy of Dermatology lists facial, nasal and orbital fractures, nerve pain, numbness and eye injury, and Vice quotes oral and maxillofacial surgeon Lee Kojanis calling it 'deeply concerning and medically unsound.'[5][6] Those sources address impact, not traction.

Mainstream coverage has concentrated on mewing and bonesmashing rather than belt pulling. Mewing coverage includes The Guardian in 2019 and TikTok-focused reporting in 2023 and 2024, and the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw.[9] Wikipedia lists a 2019 commentary and a 2021 editorial in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery on social-media alternatives to jaw surgery.[9] Maxillofacial surgeons and dermatologists quoted in the press describe facial bone as not reliably reshaped by self-applied force.[5][6]
Wikipedia's account of palatal expansion says treatment after the peak growth spurt produces more dental than skeletal change, and that skeletal change depends on age and anchorage.[13]
No studies found. Related research covers supervised protraction facemask treatment in growing patients, summarised above.[4][4]

lore.intro: Belt pulling appears in looksmax.org threads as a more intense relative of mewing, discussed for rotated maxilla and midface concerns, with replies split between curiosity, caution and mockery.[1][2]

timeline.event: Julius Wolff publishes his work on bone remodelling, the basis of Wolff's law that proponents of bone-reshaping routines cite.[10]
Meta-analysis of three randomised trials reports short-term skeletal change with facemask treatment in growing patients, including counterclockwise rotation of the maxillary plane.[4]
Interest in mewing rises in January and The Guardian covers it as a YouTube craze in March.[9]
Mike Mew faces a misconduct hearing reported in November.[9]
Systematic review of 14 studies reports short-term stability and stable long-term maxillary effects after facemask therapy.[4]
Mike Mew is struck from the UK dental register; a Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery paper calls bonesmashing an urgent concern.[6][9]
Vice publishes a March article on bonesmashing; surgeons quoted warn of fractures and nerve injury.[6]
